Migrate

MY-grayt -- built on the Latin root for 'to move.' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To migrate is to move from one region, habitat, or country to another, often seasonally or permanently.

Each winter, entire flocks of geese migrate south along the same ancient route.

Worked Example

Every autumn, herds of wildebeest travel hundreds of miles across the plains of East Africa, following the rains to reach fresh grazing land before circling back the following year.

That large-scale seasonal journey to a new habitat, often repeated year after year, is exactly what it means to migrate. Unlike 'wander,' which can be aimless, migrate implies a purposeful, often instinctual journey.

How Migrate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

relocate

relocate: to move to a new place

resettle

Antonyms

settle

How Strong Is It? — relocate → migrate → resettle

relocate vs. migrate

relocate vs. migrate: Relocate is a more general, everyday word than migrate -- relocate can describe a single move by one person or company, while migrate often implies a larger, seasonal, or instinctual movement, especially of animals or populations.

resettle vs. migrate

resettle vs. migrate: Resettle can feel more permanent than migrate: migrate often implies a movement that may repeat seasonally, while resettle suggests establishing a new, lasting home.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of migrate.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — migr-

root — migr-: to move, to wander (Latin (migrare))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin migrare meant 'to move from one place to another,' and the suffix -ate marks it as a verb. To migrate is simply that act of relocating -- geese flying south, or people moving to a new country.

Use the root in a new word: emigrate

Use the root in a new word: emigrate: Her grandparents emigrated from their homeland in search of better opportunities.
